topic: J. Ridley Stroop (1935): Why You Cannot Stop Reading the Word 'RED' Printed in Blue Ink
visual_mode_reason: Stroop's 1935 stopwatch ink-naming collision (74.3% slower!) is an iconic behavioral demonstration whose neural conflict detector — dorsal anterior cingulate cortex signaling dorsolateral prefrontal control — made the Stroop task the single most cited test in cognitive neuroscience.

primary_case.title: John Ridley Stroop's 1935 George Peabody College 3-experiment Color-Word Interference dissertation
primary_case.place: Jesup Psychological Laboratory, George Peabody College for Teachers (now Vanderbilt), Nashville

people.name: J. Ridley Stroop
people.role: Nashville doctoral student who hand-printed 100 incongruent color words on white cardstock and timed 70 undergraduates with a stopwatch in 1935 — then left research psychology to teach biblical studies.

people.name: Colin M. MacLeod
people.role: Cognitive psychologist whose monumental 1991 review synthesized 55 years and 700+ replications of the Stroop Effect

people.name: Jonathan D. Cohen & Matthew Botvinick
people.role: Neuroscientists who modeled automatic reading vs controlled color naming and pinpointed anterior cingulate conflict monitoring

core_facts.fact: In 1935 at George Peabody College in Nashville, doctoral student J. Ridley Stroop tested college undergraduates across 3 elegant cardstock-and-stopwatch experiments using 10×10 grids of 100 items printed in red, blue, green, brown, and purple.

Experiment 1 carried the first shock: reading color WORDS aloud when printed in mismatched ink ('RED' in blue ink) took 43.3 seconds vs 41.0 seconds in black ink — virtually ZERO interference (+2.3 s, just 5.6%).

Experiment 2 flipped the instruction — ignore the word and name ONLY the INK COLOR across 100 mismatched words — and human brains jammed. Naming solid color squares took 63.3 seconds, whereas naming ink on mismatched words shot up to 110.3 seconds: a massive +47.0-second (+74.3%) slowdown across 70 students, with EVERY SINGLE participant slowed down.

In Experiment 3, Stroop gave 32 students 8 consecutive days of intensive ink-naming practice: interference shrank with training, and on Day 9 a brief 'Reverse Stroop' appeared where newly strengthened ink naming momentarily slowed word reading.

Preschoolers who cannot yet read breeze through mismatched Stroop cards with zero slowdown; interference spikes abruptly in 1st-2nd grade the moment reading becomes automatic, then climbs again in older adulthood as prefrontal inhibition weakens.

Cold-War legend (partially inspired by bilingual Stroop labs like Dalrymple-Alford & Preston/Lambert) noted you suffer heaviest Stroop lag in a language you actually read fluently — you can pretend not to know Russian, unless 'КРАСНЫЙ' (RED) printed in blue ink delays your voice by 200 milliseconds.

Why didn't 'word reading wins a simple speed race' explain everything? Delaying the word slightly AFTER the color patch appears STILL causes interference — proving lifelong reading practice forged a thick highway (pathway strength, Cohen et al. 1990) that overrides less-practiced ink naming unless anterior cingulate and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex actively brake it.

Ironically, J. Ridley Stroop published almost nothing else in experimental psychology after 1938, spending decades as a quiet college registrar and Bible professor unaware his dissertation would become one of the 10 most cited papers in psychology history.

In J. Ridley Stroop's (1935) Experiment 2 across 70 college undergraduates, incongruent color-word ink naming slowed mean completion time by 74.3% (about 74%, adding 47.0 seconds from 63.3 s on solid color squares to 110.3 s on mismatched words).

wow_facts.fact: Every literate viewer watching the screen can prove it in 3 seconds: try shouting the INK COLOR of 'BLUE' printed in red, 'GREEN' printed in yellow, 'RED' printed in blue — 70 out of 70 people in Stroop's 1935 room stumbled, slowing down by a staggering 74.3%.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Literacy rewired your visual cortex so deeply you CANNOT turn reading off on command.

wow_facts.fact: Flip the instruction — read the WORDS aloud while ignoring mismatched ink (Stroop Experiment 1) — and interference vanishes to 5.6%. It is a brutal one-way street.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Automatic highways crush unpracticed dirt roads.

wow_facts.fact: A 4-year-old who hasn't learned to read beats an Ivy League professor on the Stroop interference ratio because the child sees pure color without an automatic word highway hijacking their mouth.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Sometimes expertise creates an unbreakable cognitive reflex.

wow_facts.fact: Claim you don't speak a foreign language, and mismatched color words in that script immediately betray your fluency by lagging your ink-naming reaction time.
wow_facts.why_surprising: You cannot fake turning off an automatic language highway.

misconceptions.myth: Stroop interference happens simply because eyes read words faster than eyes see color ('horse-race myth').
misconceptions.truth: Even if the color patch flashes BEFORE the word appears, interference still strikes — it is lifetime pathway strength (millions of read words vs rarely naming ink aloud), not raw sensory speed, as Stroop's own 8-day Reverse-Stroop training proved.

misconceptions.myth: High willpower lets you completely shut off reading the word.
misconceptions.truth: Even under huge cash incentives, healthy literate adults still show robust Stroop cost unless they physically blur their eyes or stare at a single corner pixel.

misconceptions.myth: J. Ridley Stroop spent his life famous for the Stroop test.
misconceptions.truth: His 1935 paper drew modest attention until the 1960s cognitive revolution; Stroop spent his career as a quiet registrar and professor at David Lipscomb College.

everyday_hooks: Pressing a green button labeled 'DELETE / CANCEL' by mistake because color and text shouted opposite commands.
Watching a toddler name ink colors effortlessly while adults stammer and laugh at the exact same card.
Feeling mentally drained at 4 p.m. after a day of suppressing automatic habits and phone notifications.
